title: the-beater-holds-the-claim
intention: The process beating is the process holding the claim, and a mismatch is a permanent loud record rather than something a human happens to notice.
why: On 2026-08-18 two ground loops held the device's address for roughly 80 minutes - pid 4190113 holding the flock on devices/ground_loop/0/run.lock while pid 973171 did the beating - and the only reason anyone knows is that Akien looked. The singleton guard is not what failed: claim_singleton takes fcntl.flock(LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB) in one syscall, the kernel releases it when the holder dies, and main() claims BEFORE constructing the device, so a loop started through the runner cannot be a second loop. What the guard cannot cover is a beater that never went through the runner - and nothing anywhere compares the two. The invariant was already half-instrumented on both sides for the whole incident: the beat writes its pid into liveness.json every second, and the kernel has named the flock holder in /proc/locks all along. Nothing had to be built to KNOW there were two loops; something had to be built to LOOK.
traces_to: Law 3 and Law 10 together: the condition WAS measurable the whole time it went unmeasured - two numbers, both already on the machine - so 'nobody noticed' was never a fact about the world, it was an instrument nobody built. And Law 7: an error is loud at diagnostic surfaces and permanent in records of truth; a duplicate loop is currently loud nowhere.

falsifier.proves_green: code-seam's invariant pair plus its class gates. PROVE GATE: the tester runs the node's proof, verdict and seal from the same hand. The non-hollow tooth is the INDUCED MISMATCH - the proof manufactures the condition (a claimant that is not the beater, under an isolated instance root) and asserts the record appears naming both pids. A hollow build that always reported 'match' passes a happy-path test and fails this one, which is why the fixture is the tooth rather than a green on a healthy host. Second tooth: with /proc/locks made unreadable, the probe reports inability, not green. DURABILITY GATE: not done until tested AND committed. FEEDS BACK TO ORIGIN ON FAILURE: a red routes to this node; a mismatch found in the WILD routes to the trouble lane, which is the node's own output path.
falsifier.proves_red: DONE when a deliberately induced mismatch - a second beater started without the runner's claim, under an isolated instance root so the instrument does not seed the tree it reads - produces a permanent record naming BOTH pids, within one beat of the condition existing, with nobody looking. WRONG INTENT if it becomes a KILLER: this node makes the condition loud, it does not arbitrate who dies. Killing the wrong one of two loops is worse than knowing there are two. Also wrong if the check migrates into the guard - the guard's job is the claim, and a claimant cannot audit a beater it never met.
falsifier.horizon: the same day the probe lands - no clock, no live host, no waiting for a recurrence. The induced mismatch is a fixture, which is what keeps this from being a watch provable only by the incident happening again.

how: The claim holder is a two-line kernel read: stat the lock for its inode, find that inode in /proc/locks, which names the holding pid directly. MEASURED 2026-08-18: inode 29118926 -> 'FLOCK ADVISORY WRITE 360391', and 360391 is exactly the pid liveness.json carries. The probe asks the kernel who holds the claim, reads the pid the beat itself wrote, and compares - three outcomes, and the third is what this node exists for: they match (green); nobody holds the lock while liveness is fresh (a beater outside the runner, loud); a DIFFERENT pid holds it than the one beating (the 80-minute condition, loud and permanent through the trouble lane). It berths as a ground_loop probe so it rides the beat it is about and needs no clock of its own, and it reports INABILITY rather than green when it cannot read /proc/locks.
